prompt: Let $f(x) = x^2 + 1$ for $x < 2$ and $f(x) = 3x - k$ for $x \ge 2$. For what value of $k$ does $\lim_{x \to 2} f(x)$ exist?
hint: The limit exists only if the left piece and the right piece are heading to the same height at $x = 2$.

hints.text: The limit exists only if the left piece and the right piece are heading to the same height at $x = 2$.

hints.title: 🪜 Try a simpler one
hints.text: Warm up: $f(x) = x$ for $x < 2$ and $f(x) = x + k$ for $x \ge 2$. Left side heads to $2$, right side to $2 + k$. Matching them forces $k = 0$. Same method here.
Left-hand limit: $2^2 + 1 = 5$. Right-hand limit: $3(2) - k = 6 - k$. Set them equal.

explanation: For the limit to exist the sides must agree: $6 - k = 5$, so $k = 1$.

alternativeExplanations.title: Check it with the fix in place
steps: With $k = 1$ the right piece is $3x - 1$, and at $x = 2$ it gives $5$.
The left piece also heads to $5$. The two graphs meet at $(2, 5)$ — no gap, no jump.
Any other $k$ would leave a jump of size $|k - 1|$ at $x = 2$.
